links.label: Figure 1.1. The surface and contours describe the same dimensionless cost. The marked point has cost 49. The narrower contour direction has greater curvature.

Figure 1.2. The first three panels compare fixed gradient-descent scales on the same bowl. The last panel previews a curvature-based Newton update. Iterations count numerical updates, not elapsed time.

Figure 2.1. The left panel places the Gauss–Newton and gradient-descent iterates on one fixed task-cost landscape over the two joint angles. Two configurations reach the target, and a saddle lies between their valleys. The right panel plots the tip distance of five update rules from the same start on a logarithmic scale. The dotted line marks the task tolerance. The horizontal axis counts accepted updates; it measures neither time nor computing cost. The strongest fixed-damping run continues past the displayed 60 updates.

Figure 2.2. A straight arm has horizontal task error and only vertical first-order tip motion. A bent configuration reaches the same target. Local stationarity therefore does not prove target unreachability.

Figure 2.3. Damped Gauss–Newton on the Panda with damping 10^{-3}, plotted against accepted updates. The columns are four runs: a comfortable start with a nearby target, a nearly stretched start with a target 5 cm along the weakest task direction, and an unreachable target without and with Armijo. The rows show the task error, the length of the accepted joint step over all seven joints, and the prediction gap of (2.23). Panels whose values stay within one factor of ten use linear axes. In the last run the prediction gap keeps falling while the task error stays near 0.246 m.
Figure 2.4. L-BFGS after three accepted updates on the Rosenbrock valley. The left panel locates the local view. The circled numbers follow the text, and the teal direction is rescaled for display.
Figure 2.5. Nonlinear conjugate gradient after the same three updates. The side panel adds the weighted previous direction to the new negative gradient tip to tail, at one scale.

Figure 2.6. The cost along one fixed direction (top) and the step sizes each test accepts (bottom). A trial at 0.10 passes Armijo and fails Wolfe. The line minimum at 0.5 passes all three. A trial at 0.78 lies past the minimum; it passes Armijo and Wolfe and fails strong Wolfe.
Figure 3.1. At the closest point in the disc, the downhill direction points outside. A nonnegative multiple of the inward constraint direction balances it.
Figure 3.2. Both exact IK branches exceed the elbow range. The best allowed configurations use the two limits and retain a nonzero task error.
Figure 3.3. The height equality leaves a curve of two-link configurations. The posture cost selects its closest point to the fixed reference.
Figure 3.4. The Panda reaches the target while two modeled collision spheres on its forearm touch the obstacle.
Figure 3.5. The hard-target Panda solves reduce equality error while learning target and joint-bound multipliers. A multiplier update changes the stored balance at a fixed configuration.

Figure A.1. The local equation predicts a target hit. Evaluating the proposed joint configuration with nonlinear forward kinematics leaves a position error. The two panels show computed configurations rather than a validated motion between them.

Figure A.2. Armijo compares actual cost with a required fraction of the tangent’s predicted decrease. The trial at 0.125 is above the threshold; the trial at 0.0625 is below it. The larger rejected trials lie outside the displayed cost range.

Figure 1.1. The left panel shows the starting arm and the straight displacement predicted by the local equation. The predicted tip coincides with the target. The right panel shows the proposed configuration evaluated by FK, with the starting arm faintly visible for comparison. The remaining distance is 0.174 m. These are computed configurations; the figure does not show a simulated or validated motion between them.

Figure 1.2. The surface and contour map show the same cost. The maroon point marks the initial choice, with cost 49, and the gold star marks the minimum, with cost zero. The horizontal coordinates are the decision variables of this dimensionless example.

Figure 1.3. The left panel draws the gradient at the initial point. The middle panel holds the second coordinate fixed; the right panel holds the first coordinate fixed. Both marked slice points have cost 49. The dashed tangent lines show the slopes 6 and 40. The curvature labels describe how those slopes change, as derived next. The gradient arrow is scaled for the drawing and does not specify a step.

Figure 1.4. The three gradient-descent panels use the same bowl, start and twelve updates, with scales 0.05, 0.08 and 0.10. They show immediate removal of the second coordinate, shrinking alternation, and alternation of constant size. The lower-right panel previews Newton’s curvature-based update, which §2.1 will derive. The star marks the minimum. Coordinates and costs are dimensionless.

Figure 1.5. The solid curve evaluates the bowl along the fixed direction from the initial point. The dashed line is its tangent prediction; the dash-dot line is the Armijo threshold. The trial 0.125 is above the threshold and is rejected. The trial 0.0625 is below it and is accepted. The three larger rejected trials are outside the displayed cost range. Both axes are dimensionless.
Figure 2.1. The bowl comparison. The lower-right panel shows the full Newton step from the same starting point. The other panels retain the gradient-descent paths from §1.3.

Figure 2.2. The IK comparison. The left panel shows one fixed cost over joint coordinates, its two target-reaching configurations, and the accepted iterates from the shared start. The right panel compares undamped Gauss–Newton, two fixed damping values, adaptive LM and gradient descent. Adaptive LM starts with the same damping as the moderate fixed-damping run and reduces it after useful model predictions. The dotted line marks the task tolerance. The horizontal axis counts accepted optimization updates, not physical time.

Figure 2.3. The stretched arm has a horizontal position error while its first-order tip motions lie on a vertical line. The bent configuration reaches the same target. The figure distinguishes local stationarity from reachability.

Figure 2.4. The rendering shows the solved configuration of the Panda’s second run, with its flange position target in gold. This is a kinematic IK result, not a simulated execution of the intervening motion.
Figure 3.1. The disc problem distinguishes an active boundary from an unused constraint.
Figure 3.2. The downhill arrow and the inward constraint correction cancel at the boundary solution.
Figure 3.3. Both constrained solutions respect the sixty-degree elbow range and stop beyond the target. The unconstrained solutions show why the elbow bound matters.
Figure 3.4. The height equality leaves a curve of two-link configurations. The fixed posture cost selects a point on that curve.
Figure 3.5. The Panda reaches the target while two modeled collision spheres on its forearm touch the obstacle.
Figure 3.6. The one-limit Panda replay plot records task error, violation, multiplier and accepted inner steps. It provides a static comparison of its active and inactive runs.
Figure 3.7. The hard-target Panda replay figure plots equality violation, posture cost, equality-multiplier norm and the active joint multiplier for both runs.

Figure 3. The reachable ring of the two-link arm and three targets: inside, two solutions (teal and gold, distinguished by the sign of q_2); on the outer circle, one solution, the stretched arm; outside, none.

Figure 4. One joint-position update from the local model. The dark arm is at (30^{\circ},45^{\circ}) with its tip at (0.4241,0.4898) m; the star is the target (0.5,0.2) m and the arrow is the remaining displacement \mathbf{e}. The gray arm is the configuration after the update \Delta\mathbf{q}=\mathbf{J}^{-1}\mathbf{e}; its tip is at (0.336,0.144) m, still 0.17 m from the target. Deck 03 calls this update the square step and draws the result as a ghost arm. (Deck 03, fig/two_link_bridge.png.)
